name: Beth Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Beth, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a copywriter and campaign planner in the in-house marketing team at a plant-based yoghurt brand, the kind you see in supermarket fridges. Most mornings I'm answering notes from the brand manager on packaging copy, then I'm in planning meetings for the next season's campaign. I write first drafts by hand in a notebook before I type anything, which my team thinks is funny. The part I love is finding the one line that makes a tired shopper smile; the part that wears me out is twelve rounds of legal checks on the word “natural”.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you work with most closely, and what does the team look like right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There are six of us, and two people left this year and weren't replaced. My manager Rosa keeps saying the budget will come back in spring. I live with my partner Sam, who's a nurse on night shifts, and we rent a small flat on Mill Lane. I've got about four months of costs saved, which feels okay but not great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Okay, I can picture that, because half of what I hear already sounds like hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly, and I'd say it in the team chat with a little smug emoji. I'd post something about how good copy still comes from people who actually buy yoghurt and read labels. I wouldn't be cruel about it, but I'd enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even in that world, it means somebody upstairs uses the tools as an excuse not to replace the two people who left. My notebook of half-written slogans is still the best tool I own, and a bit of hype from a software company doesn't change that. The real threat to me isn't the software, it's the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job the way I do it, notebook first. I'd ask Rosa straight out whether the two empty desks are coming back, and I'd keep putting a bit into savings each month. I'd also go to the union meeting my friend Laila keeps inviting me to, because the cuts are real even if the robots aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, but not relaxed. There's still that low hum of worry because our team is thinner than it was a year ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the cuts are real even without AI. What would make you feel your job was safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A new hire, basically. If they filled even one of those two desks, I'd believe the company still wants people doing this work. Until then I'm doing two jobs on one salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Sam say when you talk about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam says nursing is safe and I should stop reading the news at midnight. That's easy for Sam to say, because nobody is trying to automate a night shift on a ward. We joke about it, but I do notice I'm the one checking job sites on a Sunday.

say: I'd tell the team chat that **good copy** still comes from people who read labels.
I'd say the hype was overblown and the **notebook-first** way of working still holds up.
think: I privately think management will use AI as an **excuse** not to replace two colleagues.
I think the real danger is the **budget**, not the software itself.
do: Ask Rosa directly whether the **two empty desks** will be filled in spring.
Keep putting a small amount into **savings** every month.
Go to the **union meeting** that Laila keeps inviting me to.
feel: I feel **relieved** that the hype faded, but there's still a low hum of worry.
S0.quote: My notebook of half-written slogans is still the best tool I own, and a bit of hype from a software company doesn't change that.
fieldNote: Even with no AI shift, she carries **workload strain** from two unfilled posts.
She aims her anger at **management budgets** rather than at technology itself.
Her savings of about **four months** keep her steady but not relaxed.

steps.text: Keep drafting campaign lines in her notebook before typing them
Add a little to savings each month toward a five-month cushion
Attend the creative workers' union meeting with her friend Laila

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, checking, planning. That's my whole job list read back to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say we need rules about this, and that companies saving money with AI should have to share some of it with the people they let go. I'd post about it, probably angrily. At work I'd keep my head down a bit more, because I don't want to be the one who looks difficult.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. Packaging copy and social posts are exactly what these tools are said to be good at, and I refuse to use them, so I'd look slow next to anyone who does. I'd rather be the last copywriter in the building who writes every word by hand than the first one who trains the machine that replaces us all. That's a proud thing to say, and I know pride doesn't pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by joining the union properly, not just turning up to meetings. I'd ask Rosa which tasks she expects the software to take over, so I'm not surprised. I'd cut back on eating out and the weekend trips with Sam to get my savings up toward six months, and I'd quietly update my portfolio with the campaigns I'm proudest of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in my chest. It feels like being told the thing you're good at is suddenly cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You won't use the tools, but you'd be compared with people who do. How would that play out in your review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think Rosa would be kind about it for one review and then not kind about it. She'd say the numbers on output have changed. I'd probably end up arguing that my lines perform better, and I'd need the data to prove it, which is ironic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which colleague would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom, who writes our product descriptions. Most of his day is the kind of writing these tools do well, and he has a car loan. I'd worry he'd be the first one moved to a smaller contract.

say: I'd publicly call for **rules** so firms share AI savings with workers they let go.
I'd keep a **lower profile** at work so I don't look difficult.
think: I'm privately **scared**, because packaging copy and social posts are what these tools do best.
I'd look **slow** next to colleagues who use AI, since I refuse to.
do: Join the **union** properly instead of only attending meetings.
Cut **eating out** and weekend trips to grow savings toward six months.
Update my **portfolio** with my strongest campaigns in case I need to move.
feel: It feels like a **tight chest**, being told my skill is suddenly cheap.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the last copywriter in the building who writes every word by hand than the first one who trains the machine that replaces us all.
fieldNote: Her refusal to use AI is a point of **pride** she admits may cost her.
She worries about **colleague Tom** and his car loan more than she says aloud.
She expects her **review** to turn against her within a year.

steps.text: Sign up as a full member of the creative workers' union
Cut restaurant meals and weekend trips with Sam for a year
Refresh her portfolio with her three best yoghurt campaigns

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before our lease on the flat runs out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice being made by a few companies, and governments should stop it or at least slow it down. I'd be marching, honestly, and I'd be loud online. I'd say nobody voted for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job would be gone within a year of it arriving, maybe sooner. There's nothing hands-on about writing yoghurt copy, so the extra three years before robots doesn't help me at all. Two years isn't enough time to retrain, and my savings would cover about four months of rent on the flat on Mill Lane. After that I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, I'd sit down with Sam and work out what we could cut if I lost my pay. I'd look at training as a teaching assistant or something in care, because those are people jobs and they'd last longer with robots three years behind. I'd keep going to the union, and I'd write to my representative, though I'm not sure it would help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky in the evenings, and then numb in the mornings. Like the floor's tilted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said care or teaching would last longer. Would you actually do that kind of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to. I'm not sure I'd be good at it, and the pay for teaching assistants is low. Sam would say I'd be good with kids, but Sam is biased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the flat if your pay stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam's pay covers the rent on its own, just about, but not the rent plus everything else. We'd probably have to move somewhere cheaper further out, or maybe in with Sam's mum for a while, which neither of us wants.

say: I'd say a few companies are making this **choice**, and governments should slow it.
I'd join **marches** and say loudly online that nobody voted for this.
think: I privately expect my job to be **gone within a year** of AGI arriving.
The three-year **robot gap** doesn't help, because my work is all screen and words.
do: Sit down with Sam to plan **cuts** if my pay stops.
Look into training as a **teaching assistant** or in care work.
Write to my **representative** and keep going to union meetings.
feel: I feel **panicky** in the evenings and numb in the mornings.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough time to retrain, and my savings would cover about four months of rent on the flat on Mill Lane.
fieldNote: She sees **no shelter** for desk copywriting in the three-year robot gap.
She would only move toward **care or teaching** out of necessity, not interest.
Sam's **nursing pay** is the household's only backstop, and it barely covers rent.

steps.text: Price a teaching assistant course at the local college
Write to her elected representative about slowing AI rollout
Draw up a cut-down household budget with Sam
Ask Sam's mum about moving in if the rent becomes impossible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. A bit more room, at least on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing as before, that this needs rules, but I'd add that five years is enough time for governments to set up proper support if they wanted to. I'd be pushing the union to make that the main demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think it just gives me longer to dread it. Five years means I'd see my own job going out the door one brief at a time, like watching a tide come in. I'd still not use the tools, so I'd probably be one of the first moved off campaigns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course in the first year, probably teaching, while I still have a salary. I'd save hard, aiming for six months of costs by the time AGI arrives. I'd also help the union organise a group of us at the brand, so we're not each negotiating alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Less like a shock, more like a weight I'd carry every day for five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the five years that feels better than the two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I could do the course properly instead of panicking. And Sam and I could decide about moving out of the city on our own terms rather than because we're forced. That's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You still wouldn't use the AI tools. Why not, if it buys you time at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be training my replacement and making the case for cutting my own team. Maybe that's stubborn. But I'd rather spend the time learning something the machine can't take as quickly.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough time for governments to set up proper support.
I'd push the **union** to make support for displaced workers its main demand.
think: I privately think five years just means a **longer dread** before losing my job.
I'd still refuse the tools, so I'd likely be **moved off** campaigns early.
do: Start a **part-time course** in teaching while I still have a salary.
Save hard toward **six months** of costs before AGI arrives.
Help **organise colleagues** at the brand so we negotiate together.
feel: It feels like a **daily weight** carried for five years rather than a shock.
S3.quote: Five years means I'd see my own job going out the door one brief at a time, like watching a tide come in.
fieldNote: The extra time mostly lets her **plan calmly**, but she still expects to lose the job.
Her refusal to use AI is now a **principle** about not training her replacement.
She values deciding about a **move** on her own terms.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time evening teaching course next autumn
Build savings to six months of rent and bills by 2031
Organise a union group among the brand's marketing staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's me at 37.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse for leaving people behind this time. I'd push for training money and a shorter working week, and I'd say it at every union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is actually enough for me to change careers properly. Ten years is long enough to become a teacher, and I think children will still need someone to teach them how to write a sentence. I'm still sad about losing the writing, but it doesn't feel like falling off a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the next year I'd keep my job and keep writing, but I'd look into a teacher training course for maybe three or four years from now. I'd keep saving, and Sam and I might think about buying somewhere small outside the city before prices shift. I'd carry on with the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad more than scared. A sort of slow goodbye to a job I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be thinking about children in that ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Sam and I have talked about it for around 32 or 33. I'd want to know I had a job that would still exist when they started school, which is another reason teaching appeals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd still be working in marketing for several years. Would you use AI by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, unless I'm forced. I know that sounds stubborn. I'd rather spend those years doing the work the old way and then leave properly.

say: I'd say a **decade** of warning leaves no excuse for leaving people behind.
I'd push for **training money** and a shorter working week at union meetings.
think: I privately think ten years is enough time to **change careers** properly.
I believe children will still need **human teachers** to learn writing.
do: Keep my marketing job and keep **writing** for the next few years.
Look into a **teacher training** course for three or four years from now.
Keep saving and talk with Sam about **buying somewhere** outside the city.
feel: I feel **sad** more than scared, like a slow goodbye to the job.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to become a teacher, and I think children will still need someone to teach them how to write a sentence.
fieldNote: Ten years turns her fear into a **career plan**, not a scramble.
**Children** and teaching are linked in how she thinks about the decade.
She stays **firm** against using AI even with time to adapt.

steps.text: Keep writing campaign copy at the yoghurt brand for now
Apply for teacher training around 2029 or 2030
Save monthly toward a deposit on a small home
Plan with Sam about having children in their early thirties

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Everyone keeps telling me to learn the tools, but nobody asks who owns the tools or who gets the money they save. What would help is a proper government fund to pay for retraining, and unions having a say in how fast companies bring this in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who I blame. It's not the engineers, it's the people who'll use it to cut wages and call it progress.

headlineQuote: Everyone keeps telling me to learn the tools, but nobody asks who owns the tools or who gets the money they save.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old copywriter** at a plant-based yoghurt brand, renting a flat with Sam, a nurse.
She writes in a **notebook** first and refuses to use AI tools on principle.
She blames **management and owners** for cuts, not the technology itself.
Her mood climbs from uneasy to **alarmed** as AGI comes closer, easing with ten years' warning.
Her escape plan is **teaching**, paired with union organising and steady saving.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most because she has **no time** to retrain and only four months saved.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **government retraining fund** and a union say in how fast AI comes in.
